solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What the blessed may get — some model children

parts.note: the Model T, Ford's famous car
issue = offspring, a legal word for children

explanation.surface: A fashion shoot, and what the children of the model world are blessed with.
explanation.walkthrough: The blessing is the one said after a sneeze: someone who hears 'bless you' may well be handed a tissue.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneezer, blessed by those nearby, is likely to need a tissue.

clue.text: I can do inane dances in a wet patch of earth

indicators.note: the letters dance into new positions

explanation.surface: Someone boasts they can do silly dances in a puddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A wet patch of earth' sounds like a muddy puddle, but it is a whole ocean covering part of the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the ocean is pictured modestly as a damp patch on the globe's surface.

clue.text: Family member taking on a large Barnet business?

indicators.note: the outer word takes the letters on board, inside it

parts.note: a son is a family member

explanation.surface: A son takes over a big business in Barnet, a north London borough.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is a London borough, but in rhyming slang 'Barnet Fair' means hair, so a Barnet business is a hair salon.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon is a hairdresser's, a business dealing in hair.

clue.text: Going out snorting whiff of cocaine is stimulating

indicators.note: snorting means taking something in through the nose, so one piece is drawn inside the other

parts.note: exiting means leaving or going out
a whiff is a trace, here the first letter of cocaine

explanation.surface: A night on the town spent sniffing cocaine is a thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snorting' puts C (a whiff of cocaine) inside EXITING (going out).
explanation.definitionFit: Something exciting rouses and thrills you, which is what stimulating means.

clue.text: Cloth rep ruined this woman in Bow, I heard

indicators.note: I heard says the words before it are to be taken as they sound when spoken

parts.note: ruined is wrecked and this woman is her; Bow is in the East End of London, where Cockneys drop the h, so 'wrecked 'er'

explanation.surface: Someone says a cloth salesman ruined a woman in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is the clergy, so a representative of the cloth is a parish priest. A Cockney from Bow, in East London, drops the h of 'her', and 'wrecked 'er' is said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rector is a Church of England parish priest, a representative of the clergy, which is known as the cloth.

clue.text: Standard Downing Street stocktake

indicators.note: downing is swallowing, so the outer word takes the letters in

explanation.surface: A routine stocktake carried out at Downing Street, home of the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downing Street' looks like one name, but 'Downing' means swallowing. Stocktake is split as stock-take: to take livestock, which is what rustlers do.
explanation.definitionFit: To rustle is to steal livestock, literally to take stock.

clue.text: Material in my work upset official, perhaps

parts.note: cor! = my! as an exclamation of surprise

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns the word upside down, so it reads upwards

parts.note: official, as in the real or genuine one

explanation.surface: An official is upset by some material in a piece of the speaker's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation here, not a possessive; 'cor' is the British equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means physical, having a material body.

clue.text: Upper-class sort going topless is not on

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, the first letter of the word

parts.note: a toff is a British slang word for a posh, upper-class person

explanation.surface: A posh person stripping to the waist is unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: A toff is British slang for an upper-class person; 'going topless' drops its first letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: An event that is off has been cancelled, so it is not on.

clue.text: Unregulated bond-holders wild about a Republican

indicators.note: the letters run wild into a new order
the anagram goes around the other letters

explanation.surface: Unregulated bondholders are furious about a Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged BONDHOLDERS wraps around A R, which sits between the B and the RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-holds-barred fight has no rules restricting it.

clue.text: Is clue I do askew or very pleasing to you?

indicators.note: askew means out of line, so the letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: The setter asks the solver whether this clue is crooked or a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue talks about itself, inviting the solver to judge it, while its first four words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something delicious is highly pleasing to the one enjoying it.

clue.text: Load of work abandoned by head of government

indicators.note: abandoned by means the following piece leaves the word before it

parts.note: graft is British slang for hard work

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A heap of tasks left behind by the prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Graft is British slang for hard work; the head of government, G, abandons it.
explanation.definitionFit: A raft of things is a large number of them, so it is an informal synonym of a load.

clue.text: Attractive sort of old lady … good catch

explanation.surface: An appealing old lady is described as a real catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attractive' reads as good-looking, but here it means literally pulling things towards it.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet attracts metal, so it is quite literally an attractive sort of thing.

clue.text: One observing old knight striking person

parts.note: a looker is a strikingly attractive person

explanation.surface: Someone watches an old knight hit another person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' suggests a blow, but a striking person is simply good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: An onlooker is someone who watches without taking part.

clue.text: Gutted after kicking dearest vice

indicators.note: the letters are kicked about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is devastated after giving up their favourite bad habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, which the surface uses, but it also means disembowelled.
explanation.definitionFit: To eviscerate is to remove the guts, so eviscerated means gutted.

clue.text: Limited company with new penalty by Democrat

explanation.surface: A limited company is handed a new penalty alongside a Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limited company' reads as one business term (Ltd), but 'Limited' is the definition and 'company' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Confined means restricted, kept within limits.

clue.text: Company men bringing in a bit of trade for Sky

indicators.note: bringing in means taking something inside, so the a goes into the run of letters before it

parts.note: a firm is a company or business
a bit, the first letter, of trade

explanation.surface: Office staff at a company drumming up a little business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky' sits at the end looking like a name; it is the poetic heavens. 'bringing in' puts A into FIRMMEN, and T, a bit of trade, closes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The firmament is a poetic name for the heavens, the vault of the sky.

clue.text: Having gone the wrong way, be morally corrupt

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards

parts.note: to be is to live, exist

explanation.surface: Someone who has strayed from the path is told they are corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone the wrong way' sounds moral, which suits the surface, but it simply reverses the word next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil means wicked, morally bad.

clue.text: European schoolboy gains foremost of scholarships

indicators.note: gains means acquiring something, so one piece is taken into the other

parts.note: an Etonian is a boy at Eton College, the English public school

indicators.note: foremost of means the first letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A pupil from abroad picks up the top scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: An Etonian is a pupil at Eton, a famous English boarding school; it gains S, the first of scholarships.
explanation.definitionFit: An Estonian comes from Estonia, a Baltic state, so is a European by nationality.

clue.text: Lawyers to welcome key Russian representative

indicators.note: the outer word takes the inner letter in, as a host welcomes a guest

parts.note: the Bar = barristers as a body

explanation.surface: Lawyers prepare to receive an important Russian envoy.
explanation.walkthrough: The bear is the national symbol of Russia, so it represents the country as a lion does England.
explanation.definitionFit: The bear is Russia's traditional emblem, so it stands for the country.

clue.text: Church in Calais I renovated with bishop

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: renovated means done up and remade, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A churchgoer describes a French church restored with a bishop's help.
explanation.walkthrough: Calais is the French Channel port, here only fodder for 'renovated'; B is the chess abbreviation for bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A basilica is a large oblong church, often one given special privileges by the Pope.

clue.text: Help to turn around a crap keeper in America

indicators.note: the word turns round and runs backwards

parts.note: a = per, as in ten pounds a head

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to help turn round a hopeless goalkeeper in the US.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A crap keeper' reads as a poor goalkeeper, but it is something that keeps crap in: diaper is the American word for a nappy.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call a baby's nappy a diaper, which contains its mess.

clue.text: US trainer admitting bit of ice is extra-slippery

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a sneaker is the American word for a trainer, a sports shoe
a bit, the first letter, of ice

explanation.surface: An American sports shoe picking up a fleck of ice becomes even more treacherous underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: A trainer is a British word for a sports shoe, which Americans call a sneaker; 'admitting' puts I, a bit of ice, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sneakier means more sly and devious, the sense of slippery for a shifty person.

clue.text: Men reversing cherry-hued Sierra and Fiats

parts.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: the word after it runs backwards

parts.note: Sierra is S in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Some men are backing red Ford Sierras and Fiat cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Sierra and Fiat look like car makes, but a fiat is a decree and Sierra is just the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiat is an authoritative order.

clue.text: Ideal way to get up with energy in the morning

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means reading upwards

explanation.surface: The perfect way to get out of bed full of energy in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is advice on waking, and a dream is exactly what you leave behind when you get up.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used as an adjective: a perfect partner can be called a dream as well as ideal.

clue.text: Track one and two released by the Sweet

parts.note: a cut is a track on an album

indicators.note: one and two released by means the first and second letters are let go from the next word

explanation.surface: A record track and its follow-up are put out by the glam rock band the Sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sweet were a 1970s British glam rock band, which makes 'the Sweet' look like one unit. Letters one and two, T and H, are released from THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cute means charming and endearing, the sense of sweet for a child or a puppy.

clue.text: Exercise in American English

explanation.surface: A gym session, or perhaps a language drill in American English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise' is a verb here: to exercise a right is to use it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: exercising a right or a skill means putting it to work.

clue.text: Quiet type based for a long time in Lincoln?

definitions.note: Lincoln is one example of a president, hence the question mark

parts.words: type based for a long time
parts.note: a resident lives in a place long-term

explanation.surface: A quiet person who has lived in the English city of Lincoln for years.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln reads as the English cathedral city, but it is Abraham Lincoln, the US president.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Abraham Lincoln held the office, so he stands for its holders, flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: 100 per cent of B and A, perhaps, but not L

indicators.note: but not means everything except, so the following letter is dropped

parts.note: A is an example of a letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: It reads like a test score: full marks for grades B and A, though not for L.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A, perhaps' is a letter, and 'but not L' drops its L. After an illness, 'better' means fully recovered, not just improved.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling better after an illness can mean fully recovered, which is what feeling 100 per cent means.

clue.text: Numbers broken into by wildly keen Drifters?

indicators.note: the outer word is burgled, the inner word getting inside it

explanation.surface: Wildly keen fans of the soul group The Drifters break into the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Drifters were an American vocal group, which the capital D exploits; here they are wanderers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads drift from place to place with no fixed home.
